column2: Their departure nevertheless had to wait. There were several reasons. First, they had decided to return south by steamer, and the sailings followed a fixed schedule. The first-class accommodation on the next ship had already been reserved. Hu Xueyan insisted that everything provided for Baosen must be the best available; he would rather wait for the following sailing, ten days later.

Second, Hu wanted to take home a specially ordered supply of medicinal plasters. Ever since he had begun managing supplies for the western campaign and established a transshipment bureau in Shanghai, everything he touched had prospered. Enormous profits often came overnight; sometimes he scarcely understood himself how the money had been made. His strength, however, had gradually declined. He ate less, slept poorly, and grew thinner by the day. His mother and all the women of the household became frantic, burning incense, making vows, and performing charitable deeds wherever they could, in the hope of securing Heaven's protection. Nothing helped. Once, at a social gathering, he met Zhou Litang, a man who had purchased eligibility for a county magistracy and was awaiting an appointment in Hubei. Zhou had come to Shanghai on official business and was skilled at reading faces. He examined the company in turn, offering light remarks that frequently struck home. Of Hu, he predicted that the next ten years would bring even greater fortune than he enjoyed already: one day people would call him the God of Wealth. “To tell you the truth, Mr Litang, my strength is failing. A man needs energy to accomplish anything. Without it, the only fortune awaiting me is a place in the grave. How could I possibly enjoy a great run of luck?” “That is because you have not learned to free your mind, Mr Xueyan. Once you do, I guarantee that your spirits will revive a hundredfold.” The words themselves gave Hu a lift. “Then I must ask your advice. In what way is my mind not free? How am I to free it?” “It is not a subject we can discuss properly in a few hurried words. Where is your residence? Once I have finished my official business and have a little leisure, I shall call on you, and we can talk at length.”

Hu knew the sort of expectant local official who read a manual such as The Hemp-Clad Master's Art of Physiognomy, then talked at random to flatter his superiors, hoping to win an appointment or an assignment. Zhou's conversation suggested that he was a different kind of man. “I could hardly trouble you to come all that way,” Hu replied, then added, “Forgive my asking, but what business has brought you here?” “His Majesty is getting married this year. The governor sent me to Shanghai to purchase tribute gifts. Everything has been selected, but there was an error in the amount of money Hubei was supposed to remit. I have been running about over it for days. It will take another four or five days to settle everything.” “Ah! You mean the official funds are insufficient?” “Yes.” “How much are you short?” “A little over thirteen thousand taels.” “I see, I see. The money should arrive soon, I suppose?” “Yes.” “Good.”

The next morning Hu called on Zhou at the Xianghe Inn. Someone inside Zhou's room was arguing vigorously with him. The voice sounded familiar, though Hu could not at first place it. Then the man happened to turn, and Hu recognized Old Xiao, the counter manager at the Fang Jiuxia Jewellery Shop. “Mr Hu!” Abandoning Zhou, Xiao hurried out, smiling and bending a knee in greeting. “What brings you here too, sir?” “What a curious question!” Having noticed how discourteously Xiao had been treating Zhou, Hu deliberately kept a stern face. “Are you allowed to come here while I am not?” “That is not what I meant! Not at all!” Xiao protested hastily. “I have some business to discuss with Magistrate Zhou.” “Business? Have you never heard that good temper brings prosperity? What is all this racket about?” Having rebuked him, Hu turned to greet Zhou with warmth and courtesy, leaving Xiao standing neglected at one side. Zhou himself felt rather uncomfortable about this. “Please take a seat, Mr Xueyan. Let me settle matters with Manager Xiao first.” “Of course.”

With Hu present, Xiao was less overbearing than before, although his terms remained uncompromising. Zhou had ordered a jade ruyi sceptre inlaid with gold from Fang Jiuxia. Materials and workmanship came to nine thousand taels, of which he had paid only two thousand as a deposit. The sceptre was finished, and the shop had been pressing him to take delivery and settle the account; he had no money to do so. Meanwhile, the governor of Guangxi had also sent an agent to buy tribute gifts. Short of time, the agent was becoming anxious. Hearing of this, Xiao had approached him with an offer: he could have the Hubei governor's sceptre at its original price. The inscription invoking the nine blessings of the poem “Heaven Protects You,” together with the upper dedication, could remain; only the province and donor's name in the lower inscription needed changing. It would involve almost no trouble. The Guangxi agent was both decisive and shrewd. He judged nine thousand taels a reasonable price and was willing to buy, provided there was proof that Hubei's agent had actually abandoned his claim. Xiao had therefore come to put pressure on Zhou: payment must be made by a stated deadline, or the deposit would be forfeited to compensate the shop for its loss. With no money to strengthen his hand, Zhou could scarcely speak firmly. The wrangling had been wearing him down when Hu arrived. Once Hu understood the matter, he intervened. “Old Xiao, what exactly do you propose?” Xiao knew at once that his clever scheme had failed. “You know yourself, Mr Hu, that gold has risen again these last two days. Frankly, we have already lost money on Magistrate Zhou's sceptre. It ties up a great deal of capital, too. Every further delay costs us interest. I cannot answer to my employer for that.” “Well, what do you propose?” “I thought we could allow another three days.”

“There is no need.” Hu turned to Zhou. “This is a small amount, Mr Litang. Why did you not mention it sooner, instead of putting up with their insolence?” He took an envelope from the pocket of his riding jacket and handed it over. Zhou drew out a banknote for fourteen thousand taels. Gratitude mingled with humiliation, and he nearly wept. Hu feared he might say something excessively self-abasing in front of Xiao, which would embarrass Hu as well. He therefore spoke quickly. “Go back at once, Old Xiao, and bring the gold sceptre. Once Magistrate Zhou has inspected it and found it satisfactory, you will receive every last penny.” “Yes, sir! Certainly! I shall bring it immediately.” “Wait!” Hu called him back and turned again to Zhou. “On second thoughts, having it brought here would be unwise. It would expose you to risk and attract attention. Why do I not accompany you to Fang Jiuxia to inspect it? If everything is in order, you can pay the balance and have the shop issue a receipt acknowledging that it is holding the sceptre for you. Then, when you leave, it can be delivered straight to the ship. Would that not save trouble?” “Quite right. But I could not trouble you to accompany me. I shall send someone to arrange it.” Zhou summoned a clerk who had come with him, handed him Hu's banknote, and gave detailed instructions. Only after the clerk had left with Xiao did he begin thanking Hu. “A trifling matter!” Hu said. “Is there anything else you still need to settle?” “Thank you, thank you. Nothing else.” Zhou immediately asked how he should repay the money. “Entirely at your convenience,” Hu replied, then continued, “If you have no urgent business, I should like you to show me the way out of my confusion. In what respect is my mind not free? I am not aware of anything constantly weighing on it.”

“With your intelligence, Mr Xueyan, you would already have freed yourself if you were aware of it. It is precisely because the thought remains hidden that you are habitually oppressed.” Zhou continued, “There is nothing particularly mysterious about reading faces. Still, it takes experience to look through a face into the mind behind it. There is a thief in your heart. Until you drive him out, you cannot regain your vitality.” “Ah!” Hu had heard the saying that it was easy to remove the bandits in the mountains, but difficult to remove the bandit in one's heart. “What is this thief in my heart?” “Money. That single word. Do you not think of it constantly?” “I run a bank,” Hu answered with a laugh. “People call our trade ‘turning somersaults inside the hole of a copper coin.’ If I do not think about money, what am I to think about?” “Exactly! That is why I say there is a thief in your heart. You are a man of heroic ability, Mr Xueyan. Why should you too be trapped by our square-holed friend, unable to break free?” Somewhat ashamed, Hu considered this for a while. “I think I begin to understand your meaning. But I still do not know how to escape. It would be hard for me to stop thinking about money. I have been learning about it ever since I entered business as a boy. It is so deeply rooted that it has become part of my nature. How can I put it out of my mind?” “You need not stop thinking about it. Think about spending it instead of making it, and you will have escaped.” “You must explain further.” “The principle is simple. Suppose you decide to build a garden. That involves spending money, but what occupies your thoughts is how to design its towers and terraces, how to gather flowers and trees, how to bring spring water into it, and whom to invite to name and celebrate its features. These are enjoyable things to think about. Before you know it, the word ‘money’ has slipped from your mind. Of course, not everyone can do this. A man without sufficient means would only create fresh worries and trouble for himself. But you have no need to worry about money, and consequently no need to suffer those anxieties.”

This reminded Hu of something another man had told him. The man, surnamed Lei, came from Jiangxi. His family had served in the Imperial Household Department for generations, beginning in the Kangxi reign. Whenever a palace was to be built, they were first asked to prepare the design, then to construct a scale model from stiff cardboard shaped with heat. So famous had the family become as “Model Lei” that the man's actual given name was scarcely known. On one visit to the capital, Hu had met him socially and heard him recount his ancestors' history. The family's greatest period had begun after the sixteenth year of Qianlong, when its principal work was the expansion of the Yuanming Yuan. Once a structure was complete, the emperor would inspect it. Anything he disliked was immediately demolished and rebuilt; if the alteration still displeased him, down it came again. Building and demolition followed one another countless times. Throughout the remainder of Qianlong's sixty-year reign, there was not a single day without major construction at the garden. The treasury had been full in those days. Whatever gave the emperor pleasure, he could pursue freely, without worrying about its cost. Perhaps this helped explain his remarkable longevity. Comparing Zhou's advice with Qianlong's example, Hu radically changed his habits. He still thought about making money, but devoted more thought to spending it. He built extensive gardens and indulged himself in music and women. His former sleeplessness and melancholy disappeared, only to be replaced by another complaint: what physicians called kidney deficiency. Fortunately, he owned the foremost pharmacy in the country and knew innumerable eminent doctors, secret prescriptions, and rare medicines. Remedies intended to fortify his constitution and replenish his vitality did something to make up the loss. The restorative he valued most was a medicinal plaster with the unappealing name of “dogskin plaster.” Its effects, however, were marvellous: with its help, even taking several more concubines would present him with no difficulty.

The plaster was available only from a hereditary pharmacy in Beijing. Hu had offered a considerable sum to persuade its proprietor to move south and manufacture it exclusively at Hu Qingyu Hall, but without success. Buying the secret formula was an even more hopeless proposition. Every spring, therefore, he had to send someone specially to Beijing to purchase a supply. This year, since he had come himself, there was no need for a separate messenger. Immediately on arrival, he had told Wang Weixian to order three hundred plasters. One essential ingredient was unavailable, however, and the order remained unfinished. Since Hu insisted on taking the medicine south with him, he had no choice but to wait. When it finally arrived, a piece of news brought by Xu Yongyi made him decide to stay in the capital a little longer. He wanted to see just how far one particular man's extraordinary influence could carry him. “Take the foreigners and accompany Second Master Sen south first,” he told Gu. “I want to see whether he can get through this ordeal. Nobody understands his tricks better than I do. His Excellency Zuo may ask me about them; and another opportunity may present itself.” What other opportunity? Gu understood. If the man fell, Hu would not only be rid of a formidable commercial rival; he might also be able to take over the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company.

The man Hu meant was Sheng Xuanhuai of Changzhou, whose courtesy name was Xingsun. His father, Sheng Kang, courtesy name Xuren, had earned the jinshi degree in the twenty-fourth year of Daoguang. Beginning in local administration, he had risen to become circuit intendant at Hankou before retiring. He now lived as a gentleman of standing in Suzhou, a position his son needed him to use in cultivating connections among Jiangsu officials. Sheng Xuanhuai was a licentiate. As a young man he had studied medicine with the celebrated Fei family of Menghe. A physician ought to possess a spirit of self-sacrifice, even a willingness to cut flesh from his own thigh for another; Sheng, however, was always looking for opportunities to profit at someone else's expense. Recognizing that medicine was not his calling, he had gone to Beijing and purchased a secretary's rank in preparation for an official career. This was near the end of the Tongzhi reign. Li Hongzhang, Governor-General of Zhili and Northern Trade Commissioner, was vigorously developing Western-style enterprises. Sheng had a particularly quick grasp of such matters, an excellent memory, and an even better tongue. By searching out every opening, he managed to obtain an audience with Li, who was greatly impressed. Sheng then paid for further distinctions and qualifications, and Li memorialized to have him transferred to the Northern administration as an expectant circuit intendant. Soon he became associate administrator of China Merchants. Thus, while holding expectant status in Zhili, he remained in Shanghai for long periods, half official and half merchant, devising one scheme after another.

China Merchants had been founded in the eleventh year of Tongzhi on Li's recommendation. To counter foreign steamship companies, he proposed that the government build merchant vessels for Chinese merchants to hire and operate, with permission to carry tribute grain as well. This would provide them with a reserved source of business and prevent foreign merchants from driving them out. Imperial permission was granted for a trial. The Northern administration advanced funds, additional merchant shares were solicited, and Zhu Qi'ang, an expectant prefect serving as Zhejiang's sea-transport commissioner, was appointed to organize the undertaking. Named the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, it bought a steamer from Britain and began operations. Poor management consumed its original capital in scarcely six months. Hu, one of the shareholders, lost several tens of thousands of taels. In the summer of the twelfth year of Tongzhi, Chen Qin, the Tianjin customs intendant, recommended that Li send Lin Cuo, an expectant assistant prefect, to Shanghai to reorganize it. Both Chen and Lin were Cantonese, and Lin naturally turned to fellow Cantonese in Shanghai: Tang Tingshu, comprador of Pahe Bank, and the wealthy merchant Xu Run. They raised more than four hundred thousand taels in merchant subscriptions and took over. But because the enterprise already contained official capital and received government payments for transport, it remained a merchant-operated concern under official supervision, controlled by the Northern administration. It was on this basis that Li could send Sheng there as associate administrator.

After the reorganization, China Merchants steadily improved. Xu Run separately established an insurance company to cover its vessels, using the public undertaking to advance his private interests and making handsome profits. Confronted with a powerful competitor, the foreign steamship companies saw their business decline. Shares in the American firm of Qichang, which had once risen to nearly twice their face value of one hundred taels, fell to fifty-odd taels and seemed likely to fall further. Xu therefore conceived the idea of purchasing Qichang. Under Sheng's direction, however, the acquisition became a fraud. Its victim was to be Shen Baozhen, Governor-General of Liangjiang and Southern Trade Commissioner, who had previously served as governor of Jiangxi and commissioner of the Fujian shipbuilding administration. In reality, it was public money they intended to defraud. Sheng's scheme was ingenious. First, he secretly used China Merchants' government funds to buy Qichang shares. Once he had a reasonable prospect of gaining control, he went to Nanjing with Tang and Xu. Their first task was to win over the provincial treasurer, Mei Qixu. Jiangsu had two such treasurers: the Jiangsu treasurer resided at Suzhou with the provincial governor, while the Jiangning treasurer resided at Jiangning—Nanjing—with the Governor-General of Liangjiang. After arranging matters with Mei, they submitted a petition to the Governor-General, declaring that Qichang was willing to be absorbed for a price of more than two and a half million taels. If it could be acquired, the potential profits would be too great to estimate at once.

Shen was a man willing to take responsibility. Although ill at the time, he would not delay an undertaking promising such substantial benefits. He received Sheng, Xu, and their companions at his sickbed to hear their explanation. It was the thirteenth day of the eleventh month in the second year of Guangxu. Sheng, adept at manipulating figures, presented a persuasive argument supported by evidence, and Shen was delighted. Yet although China Merchants fell partly within Southern jurisdiction, the Northern administration had always taken the lead. Shen therefore proposed consulting the Northern Trade Commissioner and submitting a joint memorial. “We must not miss this opportunity!” Sheng explained that the foreign year ended ten days after the winter solstice, which that year meant the sixteenth of the eleventh month, four days away. The company's managers changed every three years, and the present manager's term ended on that date. Once his successor arrived, negotiations would have to begin again, and such favourable terms would no longer be available. The new manager might even raise substantial capital and revive the company, threatening China Merchants. Only by seizing the opportunity to absorb Qichang could China Merchants secure an unassailable position. “There are ordinary rules and there are exceptional circumstances,” he concluded. “Besides, China Merchants operates within the Southern trading jurisdiction. Your Excellency should both accept the responsibility and act decisively.”

Shen still had reservations. Even if the American firm were absorbed, what about the British firms, Swire and Jardine Matheson? “Their fleets are small and need not concern us. Once Qichang is absorbed, China Merchants will have twenty-six vessels and greatly increased strength. In foreign commerce the large always swallow the small. Swire and Jardine will have to follow our lead. Our former disadvantage was that we had no wharves or warehouses of our own and sometimes had to accommodate those firms. With Qichang's wharves and warehouses, we shall no longer depend on others. The balance of power will naturally change. Moreover, with a larger fleet we can provide our own insurance, retaining the profits instead of allowing them to flow elsewhere. That amounts to opening another source of revenue.” Completely persuaded, Shen ordered Sheng back to Shanghai that very day to negotiate with Qichang, reduce the acquisition price as far as possible, and settle the transaction first. The original petition had proposed joint official and merchant financing. Sheng was to raise as much merchant capital as he could; government funds would make up the shortfall. The precise arrangements could be considered separately.

With this authorization, the fraud was certain to succeed. Back in Shanghai, Sheng again diverted government funds to buy Qichang shares. After acquiring fifty-one per cent of the stock, he retained a foreign lawyer named Danwen to arrange the takeover and hurried to Nanjing to report that the matter was settled. His written report stated that the agreed price was two million taels in cash for the wharves, steamships, warehouses, docks, ironworks, all materials on hand, equipment, and other items. The remaining wharves, foreign-style buildings, and warehouses at Hankou, Jiujiang, Zhenjiang, Ningbo, and Tianjin were valued at another two hundred and twenty thousand. The total was therefore 2,220,000 taels, more than three hundred thousand below the original asking price. As for payment, he reported that a deposit of two hundred thousand had already been paid on the nineteenth of the eleventh month. A further two hundred thousand would be paid on the eighteenth of the twelfth month, followed by three hundred thousand on the sixteenth of the first month of the coming year, when possession would be transferred. Instalment arrangements for the remainder had also been agreed. Sheng claimed to have raised 1,220,000 taels in merchant subscriptions, leaving one million to be supplied by the government. He had even taken the trouble to identify how much could be drawn from each official source—arrangements, of course, settled beforehand with Mei.

A memorial now had to be submitted. In cases of this kind, a memorial drafted by the Northern administration required the Southern commissioner's joint signature, and the converse applied if the South drafted it. Sheng insisted that time was short: correspondence back and forth would delay the second payment and cause the two-hundred-thousand-tael deposit to be forfeited. He urged Shen to submit the memorial under his own name alone. Li and Shen had passed the examination in the same year, he added; Li could only welcome so advantageous a transaction. Shen agreed and appended the explanation: “The waterways being obstructed by ice, there has been no time to consult the Northern Trade Commissioner by letter.” Even if the waterways were frozen, the roads remained open. The excuse was plainly strained. Shen never dreamed that it was part of a trap. First Sheng had invoked the deadline of the sixteenth to persuade him to assume sole responsibility; then he used the danger of missing the second payment to force a memorial bearing only Shen's name. Every step was designed to keep Li clear of the affair, so that, when the fraud emerged, he could defend Sheng more easily from the position of an uninvolved outsider.

Four years later, the fraud did indeed come to light. The first attack came from Wang Xianqian, a celebrated Hunan scholar serving as director of the Imperial Academy. He submitted a severe impeachment of Sheng and the other circuit intendants managing China Merchants, accusing them of deception, domination of the enterprise, and fraudulent pursuit of private profit. Critical officials then wielded considerable influence, and the court paid close attention to the views of the “pure stream” critics. It immediately ordered the Governor-General of Liangjiang to undertake a thorough reform and investigate every item rigorously. The incumbent was Liu Kunyi of Xinning, Hunan, who had long resented Li. Since using Shanghai as his base to pacify the Wu region, Li had continued to regard Liangjiang as his own territory. Although appointed Governor-General of Zhili and Northern Trade Commissioner, he skilfully used foreign connections and the practical administration of Western affairs to install his own men in Liangjiang and direct them personally. What Liu found most intolerable was the conduct of Li's brother-in-law, Zhao Jiyuan.

Zhao came from Taihu in Anhui. His grandfather, Zhao Wenkai, had been the top graduate in the bingchen examination of Jiaqing's first year. Zhao himself had entered the Hanlin Academy, although his head was full of straw; how luck had secured him such scholarly distinction remained a mystery. He did at least recognize his limitations. Knowing that his writing would never carry him far in the capital, he used his Hanlin status to purchase circuit-intendant rank, cultivated contacts in the Ministry of Personnel, and obtained assignment to await a vacancy in Jiangnan. The Governor-General of Liangjiang was then Zeng Guofan. In the early years of the Hong-Yang upheaval, fearing that excessive achievement might alarm the throne, Zeng decided to withdraw at the height of his success, disband his Hunan Army, and foster Li's Anhui Army as its replacement. Accordingly, when Zhao reported at Jiangning, he received an exceptionally important and lucrative assignment: executive director of the Liangjiang General Military Supply Bureau. Zhao thought himself clever in everything and relied on his younger sister's husband, Li, as his protector. Zeng's successors—Ma Xinyi, Li Zongxi, and Shen Baozhen—could scarcely make him obey. When Shen died, the less senior Liu Kunyi counted for even less in Zhao's eyes.

Besides Zhao, Liu resented Sheng and the others who served in the South but obeyed only the North. He had long wanted to act. On receiving the imperial order, he immediately appointed Liu Ruifen, the Shanghai circuit intendant, and Li Xingrui, director of the Shanghai Manufacturing Bureau, to examine the company's books item by item. Liu Ruifen, a licentiate from Guichi in Anhui, had accompanied Li to relieve Shanghai in Tongzhi's first year, taking charge of purchasing and forwarding military equipment. Military merit had won him circuit-intendant rank. He had supervised the Songhu likin administration and acted as Lianghuai Salt Transport Commissioner, becoming an important civil official in the Anhui Army system. His ties to Li were close, but he investigated conscientiously. He was comparatively upright and despised Sheng's deceitful opportunism. Moreover, the shrewd Liu Kunyi had summoned him beforehand and warned him plainly: if the inquiry was inaccurate, another investigator would be appointed. “You would lose face then, my friend. Do not blame me.”

In fact, so many people knew about Sheng's tricks that Liu Ruifen could hardly have concealed them even had he wished to. Once the books were produced, questions appeared everywhere. To proceed cautiously, he consulted several knowledgeable friends, including Gu Yingchun. “The accounts show only forty-odd thousand taels in merchant subscriptions. Yet Sheng Xingsun's original report to Liangjiang states: ‘Agreement was reached after consultation on the eighteenth of the eleventh month, and a deposit of two hundred thousand taels was paid on the nineteenth.’ Where did those two hundred thousand come from?” “The whole story is false,” Gu replied. “You need only work out the dates.” The sixteenth day of the eleventh month in Guangxu's second year corresponded, by the Western calendar, to New Year's Day, 1877. Sheng's warning to Shen that no further agreement would be possible once the sixteenth passed and the replacement manager arrived referred to the beginning of the new year. The eighteenth and nineteenth of the Chinese eleventh month, then, were the first and second of January in the Western calendar. The foreigners were still on their New Year holiday. Nobody was conducting business at Qichang, and all the foreign banks were closed. The supposed agreement and payment of a two-hundred-thousand-tael deposit were pure invention. Next came the government funds allocated by the provinces: one million taels in all, recorded as transferred in full to Qichang Bank. Not a tael was missing from the stated payment. But Gu knew the inside story and pointed out that Sheng and his associates had pocketed 440,000 taels of it. His evidence? “The provincial funds were real money, all remitted through Fukang. China Merchants sent someone to withdraw actual silver and deposit it in a foreign bank. But what they handed Qichang was not cash. It was Qichang's own stock.” Gu could produce the Shen Bao newspaper, which recorded the contemporary market price: shares with a face value of one hundred taels were selling for fifty-six. Sheng thus needed to spend only 560,000 taels to purchase stock that would discharge a debt of one million. Had he not pocketed the remaining 440,000? Those two points alone provided firm evidence of fraud.

The thorough inquiry exposed the entire operation. Sheng, Xu, and their associates had proceeded in seven stages. First, they paid twenty-five thousand taels as a deposit on a preliminary purchase agreement with Qichang. Second, they diverted government money held by China Merchants to buy Qichang stock that had fallen from a face value of one hundred taels to a market price of fifty-six. Third, invoking competition with foreign steamship companies and the recovery of Chinese commercial interests, they falsely claimed to have raised 1,220,000 taels in merchant subscriptions and persuaded Shen to provide official capital. Fourth, they falsely reported having paid a two-hundred-thousand-tael deposit, presenting the transaction as a fait accompli; then, using the frozen waterways as an excuse to dispense with Northern consultation, they forced Shen to bear sole responsibility. Fifth, after obtaining more than fifty-one per cent of Qichang's shares, they engaged the British lawyer Danwen to take it over legally. Sixth, when the million taels in government capital reached China Merchants, they exchanged Qichang stock for cash at its full face value. Seventh, towards the outstanding purchase price they first advanced more than four hundred thousand taels from China Merchants' official funds. Another 690,000 remained unpaid, to be met gradually through deferred interest on government capital, retained interest on merchant shares, and insurance profits. Here again, a substantial difference between cash and stock values went into private pockets. “Deferred interest on government capital” meant temporarily suspending interest payments on the 1,980,000 taels that the Jiangnan provinces had advanced to China Merchants. “Retained interest on merchant shares” meant paying shareholders only half their interest and converting the other half into share capital. With funds shifted from one pocket to another and obligations endlessly entangled, the whole affair became an unintelligible muddle of accounts.

Before Liu Kunyi could memorialize, however, Sheng and his associates struck first. They submitted eighteen points of defence to the Northern administration, and Li hurried a memorial to court, hoping to establish a favourable first impression that would prejudice the throne against Liu's conclusions. With Sheng also exerting himself energetically behind the scenes, Liu's report was indeed retained in the palace without further action. By established practice, a copy of Li's memorial went to the Southern administration. Reading it, Liu found it nothing less than eighteen specious arguments. A powerful writer himself, he personally drafted a rebuttal. He began by explaining that Li considered the investigators' findings erroneous, had vigorously defended Sheng, and had requested that no disciplinary action be taken. The court must naturally weigh that question; it was not for a subject to prejudge. Nevertheless, the investigators' account of Sheng's greed and fraud was sufficiently clear that Liu dared not refrain from presenting it once more before the throne.

His first target was Li's account of the financing. According to Li, the original proposal had sought one million taels in official capital and an order directing the Lianghuai Salt Transport Commissioner to encourage salt merchants to subscribe for shares through allocations attached to their salt certificates. This was expected to yield eight hundred thousand taels. Provincial treasurers and customs intendants throughout the Southern jurisdiction were also to encourage wealthy merchants to subscribe as opportunities arose. There had been no claim that 1,220,000 taels had already been raised. Liu quoted Shen's original memorial: “From my sickbed I summoned Sheng Xuanhuai and the others. They subsequently reported that, despite every effort to assemble the funds, the merchants could raise only 1,220,000 taels. To meet the deficiency, they requested that the Southern provinces make every effort to allocate one million taels.” Liu then challenged Li: if Sheng had never claimed to have assembled 1,220,000 taels, on what basis had Shen written this? If the sum referred instead to subscriptions that provincial treasurers, the salt commissioner, and customs officials were being asked to solicit, why had Shen neither stated that official involvement clearly in his memorial nor instructed those officials to proceed?

Li further maintained that the officials had not assisted with solicitation, the merchants had not promptly contributed, and only forty-odd thousand taels had been raised. Deferred interest on official capital and other arrangements could cover part of the 1,220,000, but a large deficiency remained. Sheng had therefore been obliged to borrow from banks to pay Qichang; this explained China Merchants' heavy interest burden. Liu attacked this from two directions. From Shen's position, if Sheng had not represented the merchant capital as already available, but merely proposed that officials persuade merchants to contribute, would Shen have risked a million taels from the treasury on so uncertain a prospect? From Sheng's position, if funds were indeed to be raised in the manner described, what had happened to the shares allocated through salt certificates? How much had the treasurers and customs intendants persuaded wealthy merchants to contribute? Surely he ought to have submitted inquiries or reminders. Was it reasonable that he had written not a word, while willingly borrowing elsewhere at high interest? Liu concluded that Sheng had already claimed to possess the 1,220,000 and therefore dared not ask for further assistance, while Shen, believing him, had seen no need to seek other means. Matters of such importance, Liu continued, were normally discussed repeatedly, and financial figures carefully settled before being reported to the throne. Sheng's evasions could not be used to erase Shen's memorial or to accuse the investigators of neglecting the original records. When Shen discussed military funding in a memorial during Guangxu's third year, he had regretted the rashness of his advances to China Merchants. There had plainly been circumstances he found difficult to disclose.

Nor, Liu continued, did his impeachment rest on those two points alone. Other abuses were still less tolerable. Qichang had been near collapse. Even if worth buying, its assets should have been valued with depreciation, according to Western practice. Why accept them at their original value? His strongest charge was that, although Sheng and his associates had promised to remove a formidable rival and recover profits, expansion had brought still greater waste. In the fifth financial year the company had lost more than 246,000 taels, threatening to consume both government funds and merchant capital. Yet after Ye Tingchun, a candidate for a circuit intendancy, took over in the sixth year, it earned more than 290,000. Counting the elimination of the loss together with the gain, Liu put the improvement at 532,000 taels. Such a rapid and substantial result, achieved entirely through economy, exposed the appalling scale of the previous managers' annual waste. Even confiscating Sheng's property would not exceed the law, he argued; merely requesting his dismissal was exceptionally lenient. What had happened was that the acquisition greatly enlarged the company's capital obligations and interest burden, while the old vessels, wharves, and warehouses required heavy expenditure. The result was a hopeless mess. Sheng and Tang decided to find someone to take over so that they could extricate themselves. After searching widely, they persuaded Ye, an expectant circuit intendant in Jiangsu, to accept. This was the summer of Guangxu's fourth year. Following the Western accounting practice of a financial year spanning two calendar years, the company called each such period a “term”; this was its sixth. Ye dealt with practical realities and concentrated on reducing expenditure. By the end of the calendar year he had produced a surplus of 290,000 taels; by the close of the financial year in the following year, the actual surplus exceeded 530,000—what Liu described as counting the shortfall and the gain together. Sheng's original intention had been to slip out of his predicament and leave Ye as the scapegoat. But when Ye unexpectedly made the business thrive, greed revived, and Sheng's group began scheming to drive him out. Ye saw the danger. Knowing Sheng's ruthlessness and Northern backing, he feared trouble and withdrew while he could. China Merchants once again fell under Sheng's control.

Liu's memorial rested on established facts and compelling arguments. Sheng ought to have had no escape. But it reached Beijing just as Empress Dowager Ci'an died suddenly, and the case was set aside. Hu expected a decision after the great funeral observances were over: Sheng and his associates would be dismissed, and perhaps Hu would be appointed to take charge of China Merchants. What he had not foreseen was that Sheng had opened another avenue of influence, while Li had an immediate need for his services. Together, these circumstances enabled him to survive. His new connection was Li Lianying, Empress Dowager Cixi's trusted chief eunuch at the Palace of Eternal Spring. Li had originally learned the fur trade, whose practitioners in Beijing were called fur workers. Because saltpetre was used in preparing hides, he acquired the nickname “Saltpetre Li.” In his twenties he lost heavily at gambling. Hounded by creditors and seeing no other escape, he had himself castrated and entered the palace. Since he had joined the profession relatively late, he still kept in touch with many former colleagues and friends. Through these connections Sheng found a way to cultivate him lavishly.

Li Hongzhang, meanwhile, needed Sheng to develop telegraphy. As early as Tongzhi's third year, Russia had requested permission to build an overland line from Kyakhta directly to Beijing. The court flatly refused. Russia adopted an indirect approach instead, extending its Siberian line to Vladivostok, then cooperating with Denmark's Great Northern Telegraph Company to lay three single-core submarine cables: one from Vladivostok to Nagasaki, another from Nagasaki to Dashan Island off the mouth of the Wusong, and a third from Hong Kong to Dashan Island. These were completed successively in Tongzhi's tenth year. Dashan Island lay within Chinese territorial waters, but the court considered the matter insignificant and ignored it. Great Northern then pushed further, running a cable from the island up the Yangtze to Shanghai, landing it on the Huangpu waterfront, and openly establishing a commercial office. Russia could now receive Chinese political and commercial intelligence in St Petersburg almost instantly through Shanghai, Nagasaki, and Vladivostok. Other European countries enjoyed the same convenience through relay at St Petersburg. This was called the northern route. Great Northern also operated a southern route from Dashan Island through Gulangyu, off Xiamen, to Hong Kong, its length stated in the text as “nine hundred five thousand nautical miles”; from Hong Kong it connected through Singapore and Penang to Europe. At first, telegrams on both routes used only foreign languages. Later, a Chinese code was devised, assigning four Arabic numerals to each of seven thousand characters. Printed codebooks were widely sold, enabling Chinese people who knew no foreign language to use the service. Britain, too, was unwilling to leave the profits entirely to Great Northern. In Tongzhi's ninth year, the British minister, Thomas Wade, encouraged the Eastern Telegraph Company to establish a submarine route from Britain through the Atlantic, the Red Sea, and the Indian Ocean to India. The Eastern Extension Telegraph Company was then formed to continue the line from southern India through Singapore and Saigon in Vietnam to Hong Kong. Its formal application for a route from Hong Kong through Shantou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, and Ningbo to Shanghai remained unsettled. But once Great Northern opened its Huangpu office in Tongzhi's twelfth year, Eastern Extension proceeded without ceremony: it laid a cable from Hong Kong through Fuzhou to Baoshan, connected it to the British concession in Shanghai, and opened for business.

Sheng had long recognized the future of an instrument that could carry a message across ten thousand miles in an instant, almost as though the correspondents were face to face. Building landlines in the interior, however, was difficult. The greatest obstacle was the belief that they disturbed people's feng shui. Conflict was certain; even poles and wires successfully installed might later be pulled down or cut. His ambition had therefore exceeded his means. In Guangxu's fifth year, an opportunity finally arose. Negotiations over Ili had severely strained relations between China and Russia. Besides the northwest, the northeast and Korea were unsettled. Surveying the military situation, Li saw that an opponent equipped with telegraphs could obtain intelligence and seize the initiative, leaving China a move behind before fighting even began. He accepted Sheng's proposal to employ technicians from Great Northern and build a landline from the Dagu and Beitang coastal forts to the Northern administration's office in Tianjin. Its trial use for military communications proved successful. Sheng naturally proposed a further step: a landline between Tianjin and Shanghai. In the seventh month of Guangxu's sixth year, Li memorialized that speed was essential in war. Besides studying firearms and artillery, Western nations used fast steamers on water and locomotives on land to traverse enormous distances. Telegraphy carried military intelligence across the oceans, bringing countries as close as neighbouring households, whether exchanging friendly courtesies in peace or confronting one another in war. Russia and Japan had adopted the same methods. Telegraph connections now linked foreign countries with Shanghai, allowing questions and answers to pass almost instantly. China alone still depended on relay couriers. Even urgent dispatches travelling six hundred li a day fell hopelessly behind.

The clearest example was a telegram from Zeng Jize in Russia: it took only one day to reach Shanghai, but another six or seven days to reach Beijing by steamer. If the sea route was unavailable, even the fastest overland relay required ten days. Thus the two-thousand-odd li from Shanghai to Beijing took ten times as long as the tens of thousands of li from Russia to Shanghai. The telegraph's speed was almost beyond imagination. For its military value, Li cited the line from the Dagu and Beitang forts to Tianjin: orders could summon the various camps and receive responses in moments. Those words held immense appeal for Prince Chun. He fully supported Li's request, thereby accepting Sheng's plan. The Tianjin–Shanghai landline was approved, with Sheng naturally placed in charge of preparations.

The China Merchants fraud was then about to erupt. Sheng understood that successful construction of the inland telegraph could earn enough merit to offset his offences. But he had to move quickly and begin many activities simultaneously, making the undertaking so complicated that only he could manage it and a replacement would be unable to take hold. Even if a penalty were imposed, it could not then be enforced immediately. If enforcement of the penalty could be delayed until the enterprise succeeded, Li could request a reward that would cancel it. Sheng therefore established the General Telegraph Administration at Tianjin. On receiving appointment as its director, he immediately went to Shanghai to engage Danish instructors, opened a telegraph school in Tianjin, and ordered machinery abroad. Reports every three days and proposals every five created a tremendous appearance of activity. The most important task, surveying the route, could proceed more slowly. He knew it would be troublesome and did not wish to provoke a chorus of opposition at the outset. Better to wait until the equipment had arrived, the personnel were trained, and everything was ready except the wires. An imperial decree could then require the governors and viceroys along the route to carry the project through in earnest, removing every obstruction.

Hu's judgments were usually seven or eight parts certain. He believed that even if Sheng survived the immediate crisis, he would certainly lose his directorship of the General Telegraph Administration. This time, however, his prediction failed completely. The news again came through Xu Yongyi: Cixi had put Liu's memorial away in a drawer. Provincial memorials were delivered by the provinces' capital dispatch officers directly to the Inner Memorial Office, which presented them to the sovereign in yellow boxes. At present they went to the Palace of Eternal Spring for Cixi to read first. She marked the thick, soft paper with her fingernail, and the office's eunuchs interpreted the marks and wrote the appropriate responses in vermilion: “Noted,” “Let the ministry take note,” “Refer for deliberation,” or, on a memorial inquiring after her health, simply “Peace.” Important matters were invariably referred to the Grand Council for deliberation and a report. They were handed to the secretary on duty early the next morning as “morning business.” If a memorial was retained in the palace and never came down with the morning business, the Grand Council had no official knowledge of it and could not inquire after it. Of course, its members could also pretend ignorance and deliberately refrain from asking. Sheng had paid his way throughout the Council, so nobody mentioned Liu's reply at all. Some attributed Cixi's decisive suppression of the case to Li Lianying. Xu, however, said it was Prince Chun's protection that had made the difference; and the prince had exerted himself chiefly because of Sheng's formidable powers of persuasion.

On Li Lianying's recommendation, Prince Chun received Sheng at his residence by Taiping Lake inside Xuanwu Gate. Since Guangxu's accession, Chun had occupied the sensitive position of the emperor's natural father. Fearing that he might behave like a retired emperor, close imperial relatives and senior ministers had agreed that he should not participate in government. He had been left with little to do beyond commanding the Shenji Camp. After six years of inactivity, he naturally longed for action. Now Ci'an was dead, Cixi held sole power, and Prince Gong, after twenty years at the centre of government, seemed weary of his responsibilities. Chun's opportunity to replace him appeared near. If he took over the Grand Council, he would surely take over the Zongli Yamen too. Foreign affairs were the most pressing business of the day. He had heard that Sheng possessed unusual ability in this field, and that the telegraph was an exceptionally effective means of seeing and hearing at a distance. How it worked remained obscure to him. When Li Hongzhang praised Sheng's ability and tireless preparations for the telegraph administration, Chun readily said he would like to talk to him. Sheng had never met the prince, but had long cultivated a trusted retainer, Secretary Zhang. Gifts arrived at every festival and New Year: not necessarily expensive, but numerous, varied, and often novel, displaying attentive goodwill. Zhang therefore liked him and gave him two special warnings before the audience. First, Chun differed from Gong: Gong believed China must learn from the West, whereas Chun did not believe Chinese people inferior to foreigners. Second, although Chun loved military matters, he also considered himself well read and accomplished in poetry and prose. Sheng must take care not to suggest that he regarded the prince as a soldier without literary distinction. Sheng understood perfectly. He remembered that Weng Tonghe, Minister of Works and imperial tutor, whom he knew socially, was close to Chun and often exchanged poems with him. He obtained copies of several of the prince's poems and learned them thoroughly against possible need. At Fusong Cottage in the princely residence, he performed the full ceremonial greeting, remained standing to answer questions, briefly recounted his career, and waited for the prince to speak.

“What exactly is this telegraph?” “Your Highness, there is nothing extraordinary about the apparatus itself. Everything depends on how it is used. As the saying goes, ‘The art of effective deployment lies in the mind.’ That is all.” Hearing him quote Yue Fei, the prince regarded him with fresh respect. “Have you studied military writings too?” “Before Your Highness, how could I claim to have studied them? But when the British and French invaded, Emperor Xianfeng fled the capital on an imperial “hunt” and died under the weight of his concern for the country and its people. Had Your Highness not displayed your martial power and seized the three villains, the consequences would have been unimaginable.” Sheng paused. “Who with any spirit did not then wish to wipe away the national humiliation? It was at that time that I, presumptuously enough, read one or two books on war.” The seizure of the three villains referred to the Xinyou coup. Acting on secret orders, Chun had captured Sushun at night on the return journey from Rehe, then directed the arrests of Prince Yi, Zaiyuan, and Prince Zheng, Duanhua, in Beijing. These were among the proudest achievements of his youth, and the reminder brought a smile to his face. Sheng continued, “I have often thought that if a telegraph line had existed between Dagu and Tianjin during the invasion, as it did last year, the whole situation would have been different.” “Indeed?” Chun asked attentively. “Explain why.”

“With telegraphy, the enemy would be in the dark while we possessed clear intelligence. Speed is essential in war, and victory depends on striking unexpectedly at an unprepared opponent. The foreigners, newly landed, knew nothing of the situation and simply forced their way forward with superior weapons. Their poor intelligence would have allowed us to outwit them. Once we discovered their numbers, their guns, and their intended route, a telegram could bring the information, allowing us to prepare an ambush at a strategic position and destroy them utterly.” “Ah! Ah!” The prince repeatedly clenched his fists, as though overcome by regret. “Prince Sengge Rinchen's martial prowess was renowned throughout the realm,” Sheng went on. “The defeat at Palikao was no failure of generalship. Had telegraphs existed, the foreigners could never have enjoyed such luck.” “Let me think.” Chun closed his eyes for a considerable time. “According to you, if their warships came and our forts could not stop them, once they landed we should know all their movements and make it almost impossible for them to advance?” “Exactly! Your Highness sees far indeed. With telegraphy, not only would invading foreigners be unable to move freely; our coastal forts could stop them in the first place. If there were a line from Dengzhou to Dagu, for example, reports could pass along it concerning the direction and size of their warships and the weather. Rested and prepared, we could await them. How could we fail to hold them off?” “Yes, yes. That makes sense too. What other uses does it have?”

“One must think of uses for oneself. Chinese minds are better than foreign minds, so we can devise more uses than they can. But telegraphy can also serve evil purposes. Your Highness must therefore remember that whoever controls it must be someone you trust completely.” “How can it be used for evil?” “We must guard against fabricated news. False military intelligence in wartime would be a terrible matter.” “Quite right. That certainly requires care. What other harm could it do?” “There is another example.” Sheng considered for a moment. “Let me tell Your Highness an amusing story.”

It might amuse an outsider; the victim had suffered too bitterly even to weep. Some years earlier, an expectant circuit intendant surnamed Hu was sent abroad as a diplomatic counsellor. He inadvertently offended a colleague named Lü, who handled administrative purchases at the legation and was making fraudulent private profits. Counsellor Hu exposed this without intending to. The minister consequently requested Lü's recall on the pretext that he could not adjust to the climate, asking that he return to await appointment in his original province. Lü learned of it only when approval arrived from Beijing. Private inquiries revealed that Hu was responsible, and he hated him deeply. A man of considerable cunning, Lü showed nothing. His manner towards Hu remained unchanged, as though he had no idea that Hu's indiscretion had caused his return. Before leaving, he asked whether Hu wished to send a family letter. With oceans between them and home, a trustworthy returning traveller was rare; all the other members of the legation entrusted him with letters and gifts. For Hu alone to abstain would suggest some grievance between them. He therefore wrote home and bought two watches for Lü to forward after reaching China. Lü had purchased eligibility for a county magistracy and originally awaited appointment in Jiangsu. Hu's family lived at Wujiang, close to Suzhou. Although the letter bore their Wujiang address and Hu had said a private postal agency could deliver it, Lü made a special journey to visit Hu's father. He talked at length about foreign lands. Concerned for his distant son, the elder Hu was delighted and grateful for this intimate, precious news, and praised “Mr Lü” extravagantly in his letters to Counsellor Hu. Lü visited whenever he had leisure; the calls became frequent. Counsellor Hu also corresponded with him regularly, and they became close friends. Yet Lü had intended revenge from the beginning. Only its method remained to be chosen according to circumstances and opportunity. He understood that the better he knew the household, the easier an opening would be to find. By visiting often and becoming familiar with everyone, he was certain to obtain one. Eventually he did.

The opportunity arose from what he had learned. The elder Hu exercised absolute authority at home, and the whole family attached enormous importance to his every word and movement. Once he developed a minor ailment known as sha, and the household was thrown into an uproar. Lü observed this and began devising a plan. After much consideration, he settled on one; now he needed only to wait for the old man to fall ill. Two summers earlier, unusual weather brought an epidemic, and several members of the Hu household became sick. The old man did not catch the disease. But age and anxiety over several ailing relatives left him depressed, sleeping and eating poorly, and much weakened in spirit. Lü wrote an earnest letter to Counsellor Hu, describing his father's declining condition in detail while offering reassurance. A man serving his country would receive Heaven's help, he said. The family was devoted and cared for the old gentleman attentively; friends were available too, and he himself would do everything possible in an emergency. Hu need not worry. When he judged that this letter had arrived, and that family letters describing the same condition would also have reached Hu, he sent an eight-character telegram: “Your father has died. Decide your return at once.” Naturally, Hu believed it. The instruction meant that he should hurry home for the funeral. He informed the minister, who telegraphed a memorial requesting that the counsellor's post be declared vacant because he must enter mourning, and naming an acting replacement. On the very day that telegram reached Shanghai, Lü sent another telegram correcting his earlier message. But the report of bereavement and vacancy had already been memorialized and could not be undone. Hu had to swallow the injury. His only remedy was to ask the minister to submit an explanatory document to the Zongli Yamen for transmission to the Ministry of Personnel and preservation on file. Otherwise, when his father really died, he would be unable even to announce the death and observe mourning—an unprecedented absurdity indeed.

The story suggested many dangers to Chun. “Water can carry a boat, but it can also overturn it. The telegraph is the same. It must be entrusted to thoroughly reliable men, or secrets will easily leak. Provincial authorities should not even pry into the court's intentions. How much worse if they learn of an imperial dispatch before it arrives and can conceal their faults beforehand! The court's orders would become ineffective, and the country would cease to function as a state. A terrifying prospect.” Sheng warned himself that too much talk could lead to a mistake. He must dispel the prince's fears and leave him thinking only of the telegraph's advantages. After a moment, he replied, “Your Highness's insight is deeper and more penetrating than anything men of limited knowledge like ourselves could attain. Yet your instruction reminds me of a Western method. I do not know whether it might be useful.” “What method?”

“Cipher,” Sheng replied. “In the present Chinese telegraph system, every character has a four-digit code. There is a published book by which the numbers can be turned back into characters. That is an open code. If the correspondents agree beforehand to alter the numbers—adding or subtracting a certain amount known only to themselves—their secrets are much less likely to escape.” “So there is such a method! Is adding and subtracting rather like using a cipher grille?” “Much more convenient.” A cipher grille was a piece of thick paper with openings cut in it. The correspondents first agreed on the size of the writing paper, the number of lines on each page, and the number of characters per line. They also agreed which grille to use and where its openings would fall. Then came the difficult work. Like the concealed signals used in examination fraud, the one or two sentences that mattered had to be embedded in a long passage of irrelevant writing. The recipient placed the grille over the letter and joined the characters visible through its openings to recover the message. It did preserve secrecy, but was inconvenient. First, the writer needed literary skill: the concealed characters had to fit so naturally that nobody without the grille would suspect their purpose. Second, it severely restricted expression. A letter of several hundred characters might convey only five or six sentences. “Addition and subtraction are far more convenient,” Sheng continued. “There is another advantage. A grille has to be made in advance and delivered to the other person. With addition and subtraction, a single prior agreement can establish several different cipher systems. Naturally, the first two characters must be sent in the open code, or the recipient will not know which cipher book to use.”

“I do not quite understand. Please explain more clearly, Mr Xingsun,” the prince said courteously, addressing him by his courtesy name. “Yes, Your Highness. Suppose you assign me four cipher books called Tian, Di, Xuan, and Huang. In practice, a single instruction will suffice: for Tian, subtract one hundred and twenty; for Di, subtract three hundred and thirty; for Xuan, add one hundred and twenty; for Huang, add three hundred and thirty. If your message begins with the two openly coded characters Di Mi, I know that I must subtract three hundred and thirty from every number that follows. A transmitted number of 1,589 therefore means 1,259. The character assigned to that number is the one Your Highness intends.” “But if someone learns how much to add or subtract, is the cipher not exposed?” “Exactly! Your Highness has put your finger on the point. The most secure method is therefore to compile a private codebook, arranging the characters at random instead of by their radicals. Addition and subtraction can still be applied to its numbers. One layer of secrecy reinforces another.” Sheng then explained numerous other methods and conveniences of telegraphy. The top examination graduate Hong Jun, for example, had devised a way to represent days by rhyme headings, combined with the twelve earthly branches for months. Two characters could thus express a date: Yin Dong meant the first day of the first month, since the first month corresponded to Yin and Dong was the first rhyme heading. The hour could also be added. Yin Dong Yin meant the first day of the first month at the Yin hour. The final Yin served a different function from the first, evident at a glance, so there was no confusion.

“A conversation with you is worth ten years of study!” Completely fascinated, Chun asked, “Mr Xingsun, could you demonstrate how a telegram is sent and received?” “Your Highness need not ask whether I can. If you command it, I shall naturally obey. I merely need a little time to prepare.” “How many days?” Seeing his impatience, Sheng calculated the requirements and promised a demonstration in five days. Immediately after leaving the residence, he sent a special messenger to Tianjin to summon two instructors from the telegraph school, capable students, and workmen, together with transmitting and receiving apparatus and a generator. A temporary line was erected in the residence, and everything was ready on the fifth day, precisely within his promised time. The grounds were extensive. The garden was called Shiyuan, the Garden of Contentment; its main hall, Yishou Hall, bore a name bestowed by Prince Gong. Inside hung a plaque in the Tongzhi emperor's own calligraphy, reading “Xuande Qide.” This was a solemn place, with a sacred pole in front, where it would be inappropriate to erect a telegraph pole. The wire was therefore run behind the hall, linking Fengyue Shuangqing Tower to its east with Fusong Cottage. At the tower, Chun himself prepared a long coded message and handed it in for transmission. Sheng supervised at Fusong Cottage, where the incoming numbers were given to two students to decode.

The students were accomplished enough to recognize the telegraph codes without consulting a book. One read aloud while the other wrote. Standing behind them, Sheng watched the following emerge: “In the capital, hats and carriages abound; horses and vehicles crowd the long official avenues. Ten days amid the yellow dust, woman-foot, woman-foot, my spirit ill at ease. Who could have expected, amid the press of court affairs, suddenly to find these open woods and valleys? Vermilion gates reveal a famous garden, set apart in the city's western corner. In the east wind of the second and third months, countless trees bear mingled blossoms. Beneath the eaves one plays with lovely birds; beside the pool one peers at patterned fish. In company through day and evening, for a while I would forget the trappings of office. This is Grand Secretary Shaochuan's poem on visiting Shiyuan in spring. Copied here and sent to Fengyue Shuangqing Tower. The Master of Jiusi Hall.” Grand Secretary Shaochuan was Li Hongzhang, and the Master of Jiusi Hall was Prince Chun's literary name. Those references were clear enough. But the line “woman-foot, woman-foot, my spirit ill at ease” made no sense. Sheng pointed to it. “Is this a mistake?” “No.” “But the meaning is unintelligible.” The student holding the brush thought for a moment, struck out the four component characters, and replaced them with the two characters pronounced chuochuo. Sheng suddenly understood. The required character was absent from the 6,899-character New Telegraph Codebook, so the prince had split it into its “woman” and “foot” components for transmission. It was a small, sensible improvisation forced by necessity. Chun was extremely pleased that, on his first use of the telegraph, he had overcome a difficulty in a way others could understand. The instrument now seemed not merely dependable but congenial.

It brought many things to mind, some heard from others and some experienced personally. Secret communication had always mattered greatly within the Qing palace. At moments when gain or loss, honour or disgrace, even life or death could be decided in an instant, a distinctive method of sending confidential messages might provide warning of danger or secure outside assistance. The difference could be enormous. Chun remembered stories of the struggle for the succession late in the Kangxi reign. Some conspirators had used invisible alum writing; others had used Roman letters to represent Manchu syllables. Among the Ninth Prince's retainers was an Orthodox Christian cleric, and a method had consequently been devised for expressing Manchu sounds through Russian writing to transmit messages opposing Yongzheng. Although Yongzheng intercepted them, he could not understand them, and the Ninth Prince's plans for rebellion remained a mystery. Chun's own experience was the Xinyou coup. Sushun and his associates had separated the two empress dowagers from the princes, keeping Prince Gong under especially strict surveillance. They had therefore resorted to a painful deception involving the eunuch An Dehai: he was made to appear guilty of a grave offence, severely beaten, and sent back to Beijing. In reality he carried the empress dowagers' secret instructions to Gong. Had telegraphy and cipher communication existed, the Shenji Camp could have been summoned to Rehe to protect the sovereign, and the three villains arrested openly. Chun would not have needed the less than honourable expedient of leading men to an inn at midnight and hauling Sushun away from his concubine.

Prince Chun accordingly spoke directly to Cixi. Sheng's work as director of the telegraph administration was extremely important, he said, and nobody could replace him. He should not be punished. Even if he had committed offences, successfully establishing the telegraph would provide merit sufficient to offset them. Li Lianying repeatedly added that Sheng had a conscience, would certainly repay imperial favour with gratitude, and possessed abilities that could make him a valuable source of intelligence. Cixi finally decided to retain Liu Kunyi's memorial without issuing it. The Zongli Yamen merely sent an official communication to the Northern administration ordering Sheng not to interfere in China Merchants' affairs. Learning these details profoundly disturbed Hu. For several years he had recognized Sheng's endless cunning and known that he was difficult to deal with. Yet he had thought the man insufficiently established to warrant serious concern. Now he realized that he faced a formidable opponent. “Once the Shanghai–Tianjin telegraph is connected, Sheng Xingsun will control it and obtain news more quickly than we do. That already gives him an advantage,” he told Wang Weixian. “But there is something more serious. We must guard against his tampering with telegrams and sending false news or false market quotations. If we believe them, we shall fall straight into his trap. You must be particularly careful.” “I understand,” Wang replied. “I know people at the telegraph school too. When the time comes, I shall find a way to obtain several sets of cipher codes, and we can send our own market reports.” “Exactly. In future, we must transmit our silk prices ourselves.”
